title: How well condoms protect against HIV
answer: When used correctly every time, from start to finish, male and female condoms are very effective at preventing HIV and many other STIs, and they also prevent pregnancy. Most failures happen because condoms are not used every time, are put on late, are torn by nails or teeth, or are used with oil-based lubricants. Check the expiry date, open the packet carefully, and use a new condom for each act of sex. Free condoms are available at many health centers.

answer: It is a myth that HIV can pass through tiny holes in condoms. Good quality latex and other approved condoms block HIV, which cannot get through when the condom is not broken. Store condoms away from heat and sharp objects, check the expiry date, and use them correctly every time.

title: Male circumcision and HIV
answer: Voluntary medical male circumcision, done by a trained health worker, lowers a man's chance of getting HIV from vaginal sex with a woman by about half or more. Traditional or unsafe circumcision with shared tools can spread infections.

title: How other STIs increase HIV risk
answer: Having another sexually transmitted infection, like syphilis, herpes, gonorrhoea or chlamydia, makes it easier to get HIV or pass it on. Sores and swelling in the genitals make an easy entry point for the virus. Many STIs have no symptoms, so regular check-ups are important. If you notice sores, unusual discharge, pain or itching, go to a health center for testing and treatment, and ask for an HIV test at the same time.

title: Alcohol and drugs raise HIV risk
answer: Alcohol and drugs do not give you HIV directly, but they make it harder to think clearly and make safe choices. People who are drunk or high are more likely to have sex without a condom, have sex they did not plan, or be taken advantage of. Sharing needles for drugs is also very risky. If you choose to drink, stay with trusted friends and always carry condoms. A health worker can help if alcohol or drugs are a problem.

title: Having many sexual partners and HIV risk
answer: Having more than one sexual partner, especially at the same time, increases the chance of HIV, because each partner may have other partners too, creating a network where HIV can spread quickly. This is about staying safe, not about judging anyone.

answer: If you are pricked by a used needle or sharp object, do not panic. Let the wound bleed a little, wash it well with soap and running water, and do not squeeze hard or suck it. The risk from a needle found outdoors is usually very low.

answer: Washing your genitals, peeing, douching or using water, soap, salt or other products after sex does not prevent HIV or pregnancy. The virus can enter the body very quickly during sex. title: Delaying sex to avoid HIV
answer: Not having sex (abstinence) or waiting until you are older and ready is the surest way to avoid getting HIV through sex. Waiting gives you time to learn about your body, build healthy relationships and make informed choices. It is your right to decide when you are ready, and no one should pressure you. If you do decide to have sex later, use condoms and get tested together with your partner.

title: Can someone test me for HIV without my consent
answer: HIV testing should be voluntary. Health workers should explain the test and get your agreement before testing you, and young people 12 and older in Rwanda can give their own consent. No one, including a partner, school or employer, should force you to test or test you secretly. If you feel your rights were not respected, you can talk to the health facility management or call 114.
